depiction.subject: Museum map of Sri Lanka during the Anuradhapura period
depiction.event_or_theme: hydraulic, monastic, political and multi-port geography
depiction.period: modern museum representation of c. first millennium BCE–early second millennium CE
depiction.notes: The image documents a national-museum synthesis, not contemporaneous cartography. Run48 identifies the four blue-square port labels and independently qualifies their historical use. The asset hash was rechecked as unchanged in Run45/48.

vision_review.caption_transcription: Sri Lanka — Anuradhapura Period. Legend: capital, sub-capital, heritage site, ancient port, modern city. Scale 1:260,000; PGIAR Cartographic Unit, Colombo.
vision_review.visual_notes: The four ancient-port symbols are now read as Mahatittha/Mantai on the north-western facade, Jambukolapattana in the north, Gokanna/Trincomalee in the east and Godavaya/Godapavata in the south. The labels are independently corroborated by port archaeology and specialist literature. The map is most useful as a spatial synthesis of an inland hydraulic centre connected to several maritime facades, not as a claim that four equal ports operated simultaneously.
vision_review.uncertainty: Label identification is resolved at Run48 level, but chronology remains compressed over more than a millennium. Port function, importance and political control changed substantially over time; Jambukola's Ashokan/Sanghamitta episodes remain chronicle tradition rather than archaeological proof.

tag_review.notes: Run48 confirms the field image as the preferred rights-safe illustration. The Antiquity 2018 Mantai figure independently maps many of the same coastal anchors and remains a research comparator rather than a copied asset.

human_review.notes: Ready for human review: labels and research qualification are complete. Schema does not permit a ready_for_review enum; keep pending until explicit approval. Caption must state that this is a modern museum synthesis.

fragment.caption: Cette synthèse du Musée national de Colombo montre un centre d’Anuradhapura profondément intérieur mais relié, selon les périodes, à plusieurs façades maritimes : Mahātittha/Mantai au nord-ouest, Jambukolapaṭṭana au nord, Gokanna/Trincomalee à l’est et Godavaya au sud. Ces ports n’ont ni la même fonction ni la même importance pendant tout le millénaire.
fragment.what_it_shows: A modern spatial synthesis combining hydrography, settlements and a multi-port maritime system around an inland hydraulic polity.
fragment.why_here: Makes visible the causal bridge between inland agrarian/monastic concentration and multiple Indian Ocean gateways. Godavaya adds direct fiscal epigraphy and early maritime archaeology; Mantai provides the strongest long-duration entrepot evidence.
fragment.limits: Modern museum synthesis compressing more than a millennium. The four ports are not four literal cardinal points, not necessarily simultaneous or equal, and the image does not prove centralized royal control of the complete inland-to-sea chain.

depiction.subject: Museum schematic of ancient Indian Ocean sea routes
depiction.event_or_theme: Indian Ocean connectivity, monsoon circuits and broad maritime technology zones
depiction.period: modern museum synthesis of ancient/early historic maritime exchange
depiction.notes: Solid lines show major sea routes; dashed and x-marked zones are labelled Dhow Technology Zone and Outrigger Technology Zone. The panel credits Senake Bandaranayake et al., Sri Lanka and the Silk Road of the Sea, UNESCO Sri Lanka / Central Cultural Fund, 1990. The asset hash was rechecked as unchanged in Run45/48.

vision_review.caption_transcription: TRADE — Ancient Sea Routes; Major Sea Routes; Dhow Technology Zone; Outrigger Technology Zone. Courtesy: Sri Lanka and the Silk Road of the Sea.
vision_review.visual_notes: Sri Lanka is depicted near intersecting route arcs between the western Indian Ocean, India, the Bay of Bengal and Southeast Asia. Run48 independently verifies the 1990 book credit and corroborates westward Austronesian shipping to Madagascar plus the documented distribution of outrigger traditions around Sri Lanka/South India. The map is best read as a contact-zone heuristic, not as an exact meeting-point theorem.
vision_review.uncertainty: The technology-zone boundaries have no visible date range, combine long-lived and heterogeneous vessel traditions, and are schematic. 'Dhow' is a broad umbrella for western Indian Ocean craft traditions; outrigger distributions also changed over long periods. Neither zone should be rendered as a fixed ethnic or technical frontier, and the map alone does not date transfer of outrigger technology into Sri Lanka.

tag_review.notes: Use for the geographic proposition of route intersection and contact between maritime traditions. Manguin 2016 corroborates long-distance Austronesian navigation; Bandaranayake et al. 1990 is the panel's direct source. A CC0 derivative Austronesian network map exists online but is retained only as a research comparator because it does not reproduce the museum panel's two-zone proposition.

human_review.notes: Ready for human review: panel source and methodological limits are now resolved. Schema does not permit ready_for_review; explicit approval is still required before reader_eligible.

fragment.caption: Cette carte muséale place Sri Lanka à l’articulation de routes reliant l’ouest de l’océan Indien, les côtes de l’Inde, la baie du Bengale et l’Asie du Sud-Est. Elle juxtapose aussi des zones de technologies dites « dhow » et « outrigger » : un bon indicateur de contacts entre traditions nautiques, à condition de ne pas lire leurs limites comme des frontières fixes ou contemporaines.
fragment.what_it_shows: A modern schematic of major maritime routes plus broad dhow/outrigger technology zones, sourced by the museum to Sri Lanka and the Silk Road of the Sea (1990).
fragment.why_here: Provides a causal dezoom from Sri Lankan ports to the wider Indian Ocean and helps introduce that the island participated in maritime systems arriving from both western and eastern sectors; independent scholarship confirms Austronesian long-distance shipping without validating the panel's exact static boundaries.
fragment.limits: Route curves and technology zones are schematic and chronologically underspecified. Do not caption Sri Lanka as the unique or exact point where two exclusive maritime civilizations met; treat Doran-style direct-transmission models as hypotheses within a longer history of nautical diffusion.
